# Dump HLO & LLO computations

**HLO (High-level Optimizer)** is the hardware-agnostic XLA compiler component
that analyzes and optimizes the mathematical computation graph. On TPUs, the
**Low Level Optimizer (LLO)** is the lowest-level compiler in the XLA stack.
It is responsible for TPU-specific optimizations for execution on the "bare
metal" silicon.

HLO and LLO dumps capture detailed information about your computation graph at
various stages of the XLA compilation pipeline. Generating these dumps is the
first step in many debugging workflows, and you often need to include them in
bug reports.

An HLO dump is typically a human-readable **text file** that lists the HLO
instructions and their properties across compilation stages. Sometimes, HLO
modules are dumped as:

-   **HloProto**: Protocol buffer files, which are a more structured,
    machine-readable format.
-   **HloSnapshot**: An HLO module plus its inputs. For replaying HLOs, you
    sometimes require the actual inputs fed to a given computation rather than
    random data.

You can use XLA flags to configure and capture dumps. In most cases, you set
them with environment variables, and JAX also provides programmatic APIs to
print or dump HLOs.

## Basic configuration: Enable HLO dumps

Enable HLO dumping by setting the `XLA_FLAGS` environment variable:

```sh
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_to=<output_directory> --xla_dump_hlo_as_text"
```

Or set TPU init args as environment variables:

```sh
export LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS="--xla_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

For example, you can use `/tmp/xladump` as `<output_directory>`.

By default, this dumps HLO modules as text, at the very beginning and end of the
optimization pipeline.

## Enable LLO dumps (TPU)

On TPU, generate LLO dumps by passing `--xla_jf_dump_to` via
`LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS` (and **not** `XLA_FLAGS`):

```sh
export LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS="--xla_jf_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

### Include LLO fingerprints

Fingerprints are generated by hashing all the relevant components of
instructions, and is useful for comparing LLOs.

```sh
# Enable fingerprints
--xla_jf_dump_category_filter=fingerprint

# Enable "show your work"
--xla_jf_dump_extended_fingerprint=true

# Limit fingerprint calculation to 1-2 passes
# at start and end of LLO compilation
--xla_jf_dump_limit_fingerprints=true
```

## More configuration

### Dump HLO in specific formats

You can explicitly specify one or more dump formats:

1.  Text dumps

```shell
    export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_hlo_as_text --xla_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

2.  HLO protos

```shell
    export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_hlo_as_proto --xla_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

3.  HLO snapshots

```shell
    export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_hlo_snapshots --xla_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

4.  Graph render with Graphviz server (only works well for small graphs)

```shell
    export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_hlo_as_url --xla_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

5.  Graph render to HTML file (only works well for small graphs)

```shell
    export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_hlo_as_html --xla_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

For larger graphs, you can use `interactive_graphviz` to visualize parts of the
graph.

**Note:** If another dumping flag is set without `--xla_dump_to`, XLA writes
text output to stdout. Binary data, such as proto files, is not written to
stdout.

You can also configure HLO dumps to use syntactic sugar wrappers as op names by
setting `--xla_syntax_sugar_async_ops=true`. This can reduce the dump size by
about 20%. By default, this flag is `false`, and actual op names are used:

```shell
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_to=<output_directory> --xla_syntax_sugar_async_ops=true"
```

### Dump specific intermediate passes

In addition to the standard pre-optimized / final-optimized HLOs, you can also
dump the state of HLOs after a particular compiler pass.

```shell
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=<regex> --xla_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

HLO modules are dumped for passes whose names match the regular expression. For
example, to observe the HLOs resulting from passes related to SPMD
partitioning:

```shell
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_to=<output_directory> --xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=spmd|propagation"
```

To dump the result after every XLA pass (which produces many files), set
`--xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=.*`:

```shell
export XLA_FLAGS="--xla_dump_to=<output_directory> --xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=.*"
```

### Set LLO bundle formats: single or multi-line

For LLO dump files containing packed bundles, each instruction in a bundle is
printed on the same line by default, delimited by `;;`. This keeps the bundle
count roughly equal to the line count and gives a visual sense of bundle
packing density from line lengths.

**Example:**

```
 0x13   : > { %s43 = sshrl.u32 %s12724, 10  ;;  %s12725 = smul.u32 3072, %s33 }
 0x14   : > { %p40 = scmp.ge.s32.totalorder %s39, 5  ;;  %s45 = sshrl.u32 %s12725, 10 }
```

To print each instruction on its own line instead, pass
`--xla_tpu_instructions_on_separate_lines` via `LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS`:

```sh
export LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS="--xla_jf_dump_to=<output_directory> \
  --xla_tpu_instructions_on_separate_lines"
```

**Example:**

```
 0x13   : > { %s43 = sshrl.u32 %s12724, 10
               %s12725 = smul.u32 3072, %s33 }
 0x14   : > { %p40 = scmp.ge.s32.totalorder %s39, 5
               %s45 = sshrl.u32 %s12725, 10 }
```

This makes it easier to find individual instructions and opcodes with less
line-wrapping.

### Set LLO category filter

You can restrict LLO dump categories using `--xla_jf_dump_category_filter` with
a comma-separated list of categories. Common categories include:

*   **`original`**: Limits dumps to the initial, unoptimized LLO IR generated by
    the emitters, before optimization passes.
*   **`codegen`**: Limits dumps to final code generation and utilization
    artifacts, such as packed bundles and post*RA LLO.
*   **`fingerprint`**: Triggers LLO fingerprint generation.
*   **`program`**: Outputs specific to the final executable.
*   **`msa`**: Generates Memory Space Assignment (MSA) outputs.

 Example usage:

```sh
export LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS="--xla_jf_dump_to=<output_directory> \
  --xla_jf_dump_category_filter=original,codegen"
```

Some dump utilities render the entire string in memory rather than streaming it
out, which can lead to Out of Memory (OOM) errors at compile time. Restricting
dumps to specific categories can help mitigate this.

## Understand the core HLO & LLO dump files

These files contain the computation graph (HLO instructions) and represent the
state of the module or LLO stages at various points of the compilation pipeline.

*   **`module_####.<module_name>.before_optimizations`**
    *   The unoptimized HLO graph. This is the raw graph translated directly
        from the higher-level framework (like JAX or TensorFlow) before XLA
        applies any optimizations.
    *   **Use case:** Ideal for checking if the framework expressed your
        logic/math correctly.
*   **`module_####.<module_name>.after_optimizations`**
    *   The fully optimized HLO graph. This is the graph immediately before it
        is lowered into backend-specific lower-level IRs (like LLO for TPUs or
        LLVM IR for GPUs/CPUs).
    *   **Use case:** Ideal for inspecting optimization decisions like operator
        fusion, layout assignment, or memory buffer allocations.

### Example output files

Dumping HLO and LLO generates several text files in the output directory:

-   **HLO dumps** use filenames prefixed with `module_####.<module_name>`
    (optionally preceded by a timestamp), plus metadata and optimization
    stage suffixes.
-   **LLO dumps** use filenames formatted as
    `<timestamp>-<hlo_name>-<NN>-<stage>.txt`, where `<NN>` is a two-digit pass
    sequence number so alphabetical sorting matches the chronological LLO stage
    order.

An example HLO file listing looks like:

```
module_0007.jit_matmul.cl_963683785.target_arguments.txt
module_0003.jit_broadcast_in_dim.cl_963683785.flagfile
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.debug_options
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.target_arguments.txt
module_0003.jit_broadcast_in_dim.cl_963683785.transfer_stats.txt
module_0003.jit_broadcast_in_dim.cl_963683785.hlo_module_config.txt
module_0003.jit_broadcast_in_dim.cl_963683785.basic_compiler_metadata.txt
module_0003.jit_broadcast_in_dim.cl_963683785.after_optimizations-buffer-assignment.txt
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.after_optimizations-live-range.txt
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.after_optimizations-buffer-assignment.txt
module_0007.jit_matmul.cl_963683785.after_optimizations.txt
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.execution_options.txt
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.after_optimizations-buffer-assignment-values.txt
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.transfer_stats.txt
module_0003.jit_broadcast_in_dim.cl_963683785.after_optimizations-memory-usage-report.txt
module_0007.jit_matmul.cl_963683785.tpu_comp_env.txt
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.basic_compiler_metadata.txt
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.flagfile
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.hlo_module_config.txt
module_0003.jit_broadcast_in_dim.cl_963683785.before_optimizations.txt
module_0007.jit_matmul.cl_963683785.before_optimizations.txt
module_0000.jit_convert_element_type.cl_963683785.after_optimizations.txt
module_0003.jit_broadcast_in_dim.cl_963683785.after_codegen.txt
...
```

Some dump files represent linearized LLO at that stage, some contain packed
bundles, and some contain summaries or reports.

**Note:** The difference between `final_bundles.txt` and
`packed-bundles-post-ra.txt` is that empty bundles are removed from
`final_bundles.txt` (or replaced with `vnop/vdelay`, depending on the target).

## Platform-specific setup

### Google Colab

In the first executed cell of your notebook (because environment variables and
command-line flags are usually only processed once, e.g., at module-import time
or XLA backend initialization time), set `XLA_FLAGS` with `os.environ`, for
example:

```python
import os
os.environ['XLA_FLAGS'] = "--xla_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

On TPU runtimes, set LLO dump flags in `os.environ['LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS']` as well
before initializing the backend:

```python
import os
os.environ['LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS'] = "--xla_jf_dump_to=<output_directory>"
```

This writes the dumps to `<output_directory>`, for example `/tmp/xladump`. On
Colab, navigate to the "Files" browser in the left sidebar to view and access
this directory.

You can use all the flags covered in
[Enable HLO dumps](#basic-configuration-enable-hlo-dumps),
[Enable LLO dumps (TPU)](#enable-llo-dumps-tpu), and
[More configuration](#more-configuration).

### JAX-specific options

#### Programmatically in JAX

Instead of passing flags or environment variables, you can programmatically
inspect or dump HLO using JAX's `lower` and `compile` APIs.

Print the unoptimized lowered HLO directly:

```python
def f(x):
    return jax.numpy.sin(jax.numpy.cos(x))

print(jax.jit(f).lower(3.).as_text('hlo'))

# Equivalent via compiler_ir():
c = jax.jit(f).lower(3.).compiler_ir('hlo')
print(c.as_hlo_text())
```

Directly print a computation's optimized HLO:

```python
def optimized_hlo(f, *args, platform=None):
    print(jax.jit(f).lower(*args).compile().as_text())

def f(x):
    return jax.numpy.sin(jax.numpy.cos(x))

optimized_hlo(f, 1.0)
```

Dump HLO files during compilation by passing compiler options to `compile()`:

```python
compilation_args = {
    'xla_dump_to': '<output_directory>',
    'xla_dump_hlo_pass_re': 'spmd|propagation',  # or another pass regex
}

jax.jit(f).lower(*args).compile(compilation_args)
```

#### Dump jaxprs

[`jaxpr`s](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/jaxpr.html) are JAX's intermediate
representation for program traces. To dump them, set:

```sh
export JAX_DUMP_IR_TO="<output_directory>"
export JAX_DUMP_IR_MODES="jaxpr"
```

Learn more in the JAX documentation on
[Exporting and serializing staged-out computations: Debugging](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/export/export.html#debugging).

#### Dump all or small computations

If you want to include every compilation in a dump, including small ones, set
the JAX environment variable:

```sh
export JAX_COMPILER_DETAILED_LOGGING_MIN_OPS=0
```

### Dump Mosaic computations

Mosaic is a compiler for the Pallas TPU backend and the experimental Pallas GPU
backend. `--xla_mosaic_dump_to` is an `ABSL_FLAG` (not an `XLA_FLAGS`
`DebugOptions` flag). On TPU, pass it through `LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS`:

```sh
export LIBTPU_INIT_ARGS="--xla_mosaic_dump_to=/tmp/mosaic_dumps"
```

Or pass it directly as a command-line flag to binaries that register it:

```sh
--xla_mosaic_dump_to=/tmp/mosaic_dumps
```

Check out the
[JAX documentation on Pallas and Mosaic](https://docs.jax.dev/en/latest/pallas/index.html)
to learn more.

## More with HLO & LLO dumps

### Finding the right computation

Usually, many computations get dumped. The dumped files are explicitly named
with the JAX, Tensorflow, or PyTorch/XLA "computation name" that are called out
in the logs, making it easy to identify the relevant HLO files. For example:

```
1624325116260738.module_0065.pmap__unnamed_wrapped_function_.186875.before_optimizations.txt
```

Otherwise, you can use `ripgrep` to quickly identify which module holds
particular symbols or computations.

**Tip:** Include the 3 dumped `before_optimizations`, `after_optimizations`, and
`buffer-assignment` files of interest in your bug reports.

### Visualize with XProf

The XProf [Graph Viewer tool](https://openxla.org/xprof/graph_viewer) can help
you visualize the unoptimized HLO graph and extract the relevant HLO text in
various formats.

### HLO conversion

The `hlo-opt` tool can translate between `HloProto` and text formats, which is
useful when you have one format and need the other for debugging.

Learn how to use it in the
[XLA Tooling documentation: hlo-opt](tools.md#hlo-opt-convert-hlo-module-formats).

### Replay

You can run (replay) the dumped computations on a specified XLA backend with
fake data or input snapshots. This is a convenient way to reproduce, iterate,
and debug issues in XLA.

The following commands use fake data. If you have saved `HloSnapshot`s, you
can pass those instead, and the data from the snapshot is used. To still use
fake data while running a snapshot, pass `--force_fake_data`.

CPU backend:

```shell
bazel run -c opt //xla/hlo/tools:run_hlo_module -- --platform=cpu \
 /tmp/xladump/module_4561.before_optimizations.txt
```

GPU backend:

```shell
bazel run -c opt //xla/hlo/tools:run_hlo_module -- --platform=CUDA \
 /tmp/xladump/module_4561.before_optimizations.txt
```
